title: Two circuits, five jobs, and the vessel sequence
summary: Pulmonary versus systemic vessels, the five functions of the circulatory system, and the one-way sequence heart to arteries to capillaries to veins to heart.
objectives: Contrast pulmonary vessels with systemic vessels
List the five functions of the circulatory system
Recite the sequence heart to arteries to capillaries to veins to heart
Explain why the two circuits are in series
takeaways: Pulmonary vessels: right ventricle to lungs to left atrium. Systemic vessels: left ventricle to the body to right atrium.
Five jobs: carry blood, exchange, transport (hormones, immune, coagulation, enzymes, nutrients, gases, wastes), help regulate blood pressure, direct flow to tissues.
Three vessel types form one continuous loop: heart → arteries → capillaries → veins → heart.
Arteries leave the heart and get smaller; veins return and get larger.

steps.title: Welcome to Chapter 21: vessels and circulation
steps.text:
Chapter 20 was the pump. This chapter is the pipes and the rules of flow. Blood only moves from higher pressure to lower pressure. The heart creates that pressure; the vessels distribute it, exchange at the tissues, and bring blood back.

Start with two named sets of vessels. Pulmonary vessels carry blood from the right ventricle to the lungs and back to the left atrium. Systemic vessels carry blood from the left ventricle to all parts of the body and back to the right atrium.

The diagram follows blood through the pulmonary and systemic circuits. The aorta begins the systemic arterial tree.

check.q: Where do pulmonary vessels start and where do they finish?
check.a: They start at the right ventricle, go to the lungs, and finish at the left atrium.

steps.title: Pulmonary versus systemic, in series
steps.text:
The two circuits are in series. Blood that has just returned from the body enters the right heart and is sent through the pulmonary vessels. After the lungs, it enters the left heart and is sent through the systemic vessels. Then it comes back to the right heart again.

So: right heart → lungs → left heart → body → right heart. Each side of the heart feeds one circuit and receives from the other.

The aorta is the first systemic artery. The superior and inferior venae cavae are the last large systemic veins, emptying into the right atrium.
steps.pitfall: Pulmonary vessels are not 'the vessels of the lung tissue's own nutrition.' They are the circuit from right ventricle to lungs to left atrium. The lung tissue also has bronchial (systemic) supply, which is a later detail.

check.q: Blood leaving the left ventricle next travels in which set of vessels?
check.a: The systemic vessels, to all parts of the body, then back to the right atrium.

steps.title: Five functions of the circulatory system
steps.text:
Memorize these five. They are a classic short-answer list.

1. Carries blood to the body tissues and back to the heart.

2. Exchanges nutrients, waste products and gases between blood and tissues.

3. Transports hormones, components of the immune system, molecules required for coagulation, enzymes, nutrients, gases, waste products, and so on.

4. Helps regulate blood pressure.

5. Directs blood flow to tissues by controlling the degree or volume of flow (vasoconstriction and vasodilation, covered next).

check.q: Name the five functions of the circulatory system.
check.a: Carry blood to tissues and back; exchange nutrients, wastes and gases; transport hormones, immune components, coagulation factors, enzymes, nutrients, gases and wastes; help regulate blood pressure; direct flow to tissues by controlling volume of flow.

steps.title: The sequence: heart to arteries to capillaries to veins to heart
steps.text:
Three types of blood vessel form a continuous passageway from the heart to the tissues and back:

heart → arteries → capillaries → veins → heart

Arteries carry blood away from the heart and get smaller with distance. Capillaries are the exchange vessels. Veins carry blood toward the heart and get larger as they approach it.

The diagram shows the sizes in the order blood meets them. You do not need named branches yet. You need the order, because every later lesson is a close-up of one step in this sequence.

check.q: Write the vessel sequence starting and ending at the heart.
check.a: Heart → arteries → capillaries → veins → heart.

steps.title: Why the sequence cannot be shuffled
steps.text:
Arteries are built to take high, fluctuating pressure from the ventricles. Capillaries are built as a thin wall for exchange. Veins are built as a low-pressure return with valves.

If blood skipped capillaries, tissues would not exchange nutrients, gases or wastes. If veins had to take arterial pressure, they would fail (that is part of what happens in pathologic arteriovenous anastomoses, later).

In the model, follow the aorta leaving the left heart, then imagine the unseen capillary beds in the lungs and body, then the venae cavae returning to the right atrium.

check.q: Which vessel type is the site of exchange between blood and interstitial spaces?
check.a: Capillaries.

steps.title: A map of the rest of the chapter
steps.text:
The next lessons follow the sequence, then the physics, then the control systems.

Structure: tunics of the wall → artery types → capillaries and networks → veins and valves → portal systems, vasa vasorum and nerves.

Hemodynamics: laminar versus turbulent flow, blood pressure measurement, Poiseuille, Laplace, compliance, pressure, velocity and pulse.

Exchange and return: capillary fluid movement and venous return.

Control: short-term and long-term blood pressure, tissue blood flow, shock, fetal shunts, aging and pressure disorders.

Each lesson assumes only the ones before it.

check.q: Arteries carry blood which way relative to the heart, and what happens to their diameter with distance?
check.a: Away from the heart; they get smaller with distance.

practice.q: Pulmonary vessels transport blood from the…
choices: Left ventricle to the body to the right atrium
Right ventricle to the lungs to the left atrium
Left atrium to the lungs to the right ventricle
Right atrium to the body to the left ventricle
practice.why: Pulmonary vessels run right ventricle → lungs → left atrium.

practice.q: Systemic vessels transport blood from the…
choices: Right ventricle to the lungs to the left atrium
Left ventricle to all parts of the body to the right atrium
Right atrium to the lungs to the left atrium
Left atrium to the body to the right ventricle
practice.why: Systemic vessels run left ventricle → body → right atrium.

practice.q: Which is NOT one of the five functions of the circulatory system?
choices: Carrying blood to tissues and back
Producing red blood cells in vessel walls
practice.why: Red blood cells are made in bone marrow. The five jobs are carry, exchange, transport, pressure and directing flow.

practice.q: As arteries travel farther from the heart they…
practice.why: Arteries carry blood away from the heart and get smaller with distance.

practice.q: Veins carry blood…
choices: Away from the heart and get smaller
Toward the heart and get larger as they approach it
practice.why: Veins return blood toward the heart and enlarge as they approach it.

practice.q: Put the vessel sequence in the order blood travels, starting at the heart.
List the five functions of the circulatory system.
practice.a: Carry blood to tissues and back; exchange nutrients, wastes and gases; transport hormones, immune components, coagulation molecules, enzymes, nutrients, gases and wastes; help regulate blood pressure; direct blood flow to tissues.

practice.q: The two circuits are in series. Starting in the right ventricle, name the path through both circuits.
practice.a: Right ventricle → pulmonary vessels (lungs) → left atrium and left ventricle → systemic vessels (body) → right atrium.

title: The three tunics of a blood vessel wall
summary: Tunica intima, tunica media and tunica externa, including elastic membranes, vasa vasorum and nervi vasorum, on a muscular artery.
objectives: Name the three tunics from lumen outward and the tissues in each
Explain vasoconstriction and vasodilation
Locate the internal and external elastic laminae
Say what vasa vasorum and nervi vasorum are
takeaways: Intima (interna): endothelium, basement membrane, lamina propria, internal elastic membrane (fenestrated elastic fibers).
Media: circular smooth muscle; constriction decreases flow, dilation increases flow; elastic and collagen vary with vessel size.
Externa (adventitia): connective tissue, dense near the vessel then loose, merging with surrounding CT; holds vasa vasorum and nervi vasorum.
Arteries have internal and external elastic membranes; thick walls cannot live on diffusion from the lumen alone.

steps.title: Three coats around a tube
steps.text:
Arteries and veins share three tissue layers (tunics). Capillaries are the exception: they are mostly endothelium. Learn the three coats from the blood outward, because exam questions almost always go lumen → outside.

Tunica intima (also called tunica interna) is the inner lining. Tunica media is the muscular middle. Tunica externa (adventitia) is the outer connective-tissue sheath.

The diagram and the muscular-artery model show the same layers. Rotate the model and work from the lumen out.

check.q: Name the three tunics from the lumen outward.
check.a: Tunica intima (interna), tunica media, tunica externa (adventitia).

steps.title: Tunica intima: the lining in contact with blood
steps.text:
The intima has four parts in a typical artery, from the blood outward.

Endothelium: simple squamous cells in contact with the blood. A smooth lining reduces turbulence and clotting.

Basement membrane under the endothelium.

Lamina propria: a thin connective-tissue layer (the subendothelial layer on the model).

Internal elastic membrane: a fenestrated layer of elastic fibers (it has windows). It marks the outer edge of the intima in arteries. On the model it is labelled internal elastic lamina.

check.q: What four things make up the tunica intima, from the blood outward?
check.a: Endothelium, basement membrane, lamina propria (subendothelial CT), and the internal elastic membrane (fenestrated elastic fibers).

steps.title: Tunica media: circular smooth muscle
steps.text:
The media is smooth muscle cells arranged circularly around the vessel. It also contains variable amounts of elastic and collagen fibers, depending on vessel size (elastic arteries have more elastic tissue; muscular arteries have more muscle).

When the muscle contracts, the lumen narrows: vasoconstriction, which decreases blood flow.

When the muscle relaxes, the lumen widens: vasodilation, which increases blood flow.

This is how the circulatory system directs flow (function 5 from the last lesson).
steps.pitfall: Circular muscle means a ring around the lumen. When the ring tightens, the hole gets smaller. Students sometimes picture lengthwise muscle, which would not change diameter the same way.

check.q: What is vasoconstriction, and what does it do to blood flow?
check.a: Circular smooth muscle of the media contracts, narrowing the vessel and decreasing blood flow.

steps.title: Tunica externa: the outer sheath
steps.text:
The tunica externa (the model says tunica adventitia; both names are used) is connective tissue. It is denser and more regular next to the vessel, then becomes looser and merges with surrounding connective tissue, anchoring the vessel in place.

In large vessels this layer also holds the wall's own small blood vessels and nerves, which the next step names.

check.q: What is the tunica externa made of, and what does it merge with?
check.a: Connective tissue that is dense near the vessel and becomes loose, merging with surrounding CT.

steps.title: Elastic membranes of an artery
steps.text:
Arteries have two elastic sheets that veins lack or have only poorly.

The internal elastic lamina (internal elastic membrane) sits between intima and media. It is fenestrated elastic tissue.

The external elastic lamina sits between media and externa.

Find both on the muscular-artery model. They look wavy in section because the wall is elastic and the vessel recoils when cut.

check.q: Where do the internal and external elastic laminae sit?
check.a: Internal: between intima and media. External: between media and externa.

steps.title: Vasa vasorum and nervi vasorum
steps.text:
A thick wall cannot be fed only by diffusion from the blood in its own lumen. Vessels larger than about 1 mm have vasa vasorum ('vessels of the vessels'): small vessels that penetrate from the exterior and form a capillary network in the tunica externa and tunica media.

Nervi vasorum are the nerves in the adventitia that control the smooth muscle, and so the vessel's diameter.

Find both on the model in the adventitia. You will meet vasa vasorum and innervation again as a whole lesson; here you only need to see them as parts of the wall.
steps.clinical: If vasa vasorum are damaged, the outer wall can weaken. That idea returns with aneurysms later in the chapter.

check.q: What are vasa vasorum, and which tunics do they supply?
check.a: Small vessels that feed the wall of large arteries and veins from the outside; they form capillaries in the externa and media.

practice.q: Order the layers of an artery wall from the lumen outward.
The endothelium belongs to which tunic?
practice.why: Endothelium is the innermost lining of the tunica intima, in contact with the blood.

practice.q: Vasodilation means smooth muscle of the media…
practice.why: Relaxation widens the lumen and increases blood flow.

practice.q: The internal elastic membrane is…
choices: A fenestrated layer of elastic fibers
practice.why: It is a fenestrated (windowed) layer of elastic fibers at the outer edge of the intima.

practice.q: The tunica media is made of…
practice.why: Media is circular smooth muscle, plus variable elastic and collagen.

practice.q: Why do large vessels need vasa vasorum?
practice.a: Their walls are too thick for diffusion from the lumen; vasa vasorum penetrate from the exterior to supply the externa and media.

title: Elastic arteries, muscular arteries and arterioles
summary: Three artery classes by size and wall: elastic (conducting) about 10 mm, muscular (distributing) 40 to 300 µm with 25 to 40 muscle layers, and arterioles 9 to 40 µm.
objectives: Give the diameter and wall features of elastic arteries, muscular arteries and arterioles
Explain conducting versus distributing
Describe how elastic tissue and smooth muscle change as arteries get smaller
Give named examples of elastic and muscular arteries
takeaways: Elastic (conducting) arteries: largest, about 10 mm, more elastic tissue than smooth muscle, thick intima, thin externa, pressure swings between systole and diastole; most named large arteries near the heart.

Muscular (distributing) arteries: 40 to 300 µm, thick walls with 25 to 40 layers of smooth muscle; they partly regulate supply to body regions. Smaller muscular arteries have fewer layers and are adapted for vasoconstriction and vasodilation.
Arterioles: 9 to 40 µm; smallest arteries in which all three tunics can still be told apart; they feed capillaries and can constrict or dilate.
As arteries get smaller: less elastic tissue, relatively more smooth muscle.

steps.title: Arteries get smaller, and their walls change
steps.text:
Arteries carry blood away from the heart. There are three classes: elastic arteries, muscular arteries and arterioles.

As they get smaller they transition in two ways at once:

• from a high proportion of elastic fibers toward fewer elastic fibers

• from a smaller proportion of smooth muscle toward more smooth muscle (relative to elastic tissue)

Near the heart the wall must stretch and recoil with each beat. Farther out the wall must pinch or open to send blood where it is needed.

check.q: As arteries get smaller, what happens to elastic tissue and smooth muscle?
check.a: Elastic fibers decrease; the proportion of smooth muscle increases.

steps.title: Elastic (conducting) arteries
steps.text:
Elastic arteries are also called conducting arteries. They include most of the named arteries nearest the heart. Diameter is about 10 mm (the largest).

They see high pressure that fluctuates between systolic and diastolic. They have more elastic tissue than smooth muscle, a relatively thick tunica intima, and a thin tunica externa.

On the elastic-artery model, find the stacked elastic lamellae in the media, with some smooth muscle among them, and the internal elastic lamina. The aorta and aortic arch in the atlas are the textbook examples.

check.q: Give the diameter of elastic arteries and say whether they have more elastic tissue or more smooth muscle.
check.a: About 10 mm; more elastic tissue than smooth muscle.

steps.title: Why they are called conducting arteries
steps.text:
Each ventricular squeeze dumps a pulse of blood into these large tubes. The elastic wall stretches in systole and recoils in diastole, so flow continues between beats instead of stopping. That is how they conduct the pulse onward toward muscular arteries.

If they lost their elastic tissue they would still conduct blood, but the pressure swing would be harsher. That idea returns as arteriosclerosis and widened pulse pressure.

check.q: What does the elastic wall do in systole and in diastole?
check.a: It stretches in systole and recoils in diastole, keeping blood moving between beats.

steps.title: Muscular (distributing) arteries
steps.text:
Muscular arteries are 40 µm to 300 µm in diameter. They are called distributing arteries because they send blood to different regions of the body.

Medium muscular arteries have thick walls with 25 to 40 layers of smooth muscle. That muscle lets them partly regulate blood supply to a region: more to an active limb, less to an idle gut, for example.

Smaller muscular arteries have fewer smooth muscle layers and are especially adapted for vasodilation and vasoconstriction.

The brachial, femoral and radial arteries in the atlas are muscular (distributing) arteries you can name.

check.q: What diameter and how many smooth-muscle layers do medium muscular arteries have?
check.a: 40 to 300 µm; 25 to 40 layers of smooth muscle.

steps.title: Arterioles
steps.text:
Arterioles are 9 µm to 40 µm. They transport blood from small arteries to capillaries.

They are the smallest arteries in which all three tunics can still be differentiated. Smaller than that, you are looking at a capillary (endothelium plus basement membrane).

Arterioles are still capable of vasoconstriction and vasodilation. Later you will see that the greatest drop in blood pressure happens here, because they are numerous and can change diameter.

check.q: Give the diameter of arterioles and their job.
check.a: 9 to 40 µm; they carry blood from small arteries to capillaries and can still constrict or dilate. All three tunics can still be told apart.

steps.title: Match the class to a named vessel
steps.text:
Use the atlas as a memory peg, not a complete catalogue.

Elastic: aorta and aortic arch (and the other great conducting arteries near the heart).

Muscular: brachial (arm), femoral (thigh), radial (forearm). These are the ones you feel as a pulse more distally, and the brachial is where a blood-pressure cuff works.

You cannot see arterioles in the atlas; they are microscopic. Know the numbers: elastic ~10 mm, muscular 40–300 µm, arterioles 9–40 µm, then capillaries 7–9 µm next lesson.

check.q: Classify the aorta and the radial artery.
check.a: Aorta: elastic (conducting). Radial: muscular (distributing).

practice.q: Elastic arteries are about how wide?
practice.why: Elastic (conducting) arteries are the largest, about 10 mm.

practice.q: Medium muscular arteries have how many layers of smooth muscle?
practice.why: The lecture gives 25 to 40 layers in medium muscular arteries.

practice.q: Arterioles are…
choices: 9 to 40 µm and the smallest arteries with three tunics still visible
practice.why: Arterioles are 9 to 40 µm, feed capillaries, and still show three tunics.

practice.q: Muscular arteries are also called…
practice.why: Muscular arteries distribute blood to regions and partly regulate supply.

practice.q: Which is TRUE of elastic arteries?
choices: More smooth muscle than elastic tissue
Thin tunica intima and thick externa
More elastic tissue than smooth muscle, thick intima, thin externa
practice.why: Elastic arteries: more elastic than muscle, relatively thick intima, thin externa.

practice.q: Order these arteries from largest diameter to smallest.
What do distributing arteries regulate?
practice.a: They partly regulate blood supply to different regions of the body by vasoconstriction and vasodilation.

title: Capillaries: wall, size and three types
summary: Capillaries are 7 to 9 µm exchange vessels. Continuous, fenestrated and sinusoidal types, seen in lung, kidney and liver models.
objectives: Describe a capillary wall and give its diameter
Name the three capillary types and where each is found
Explain how substances cross capillary walls
Identify alveolar, glomerular and sinusoidal capillaries on the organ models
takeaways: 7 to 9 µm; wall = endothelium (simple squamous) + basement membrane + a delicate loose CT layer; scattered pericapillary cells (fibroblasts, macrophages or undifferentiated smooth muscle).
Substances cross by diffusion through or between endothelial cells, or through fenestrae.
Continuous: no gaps, no fenestrae, less permeable to large molecules (muscle, nervous tissue).
Fenestrated: numerous fenestrae, highly permeable (intestinal villi, ciliary process, choroid plexus, kidney glomeruli).
Sinusoidal: large diameter, large fenestrae, less basement membrane (endocrine glands, liver).

steps.title: A capillary is an exchange tube 7 to 9 µm wide
steps.text:
A red blood cell is about 7 to 8 µm. A capillary is 7 to 9 µm, so cells squeeze through in single file. That slow, close contact is the point: these are the vessels for exchanges between blood and interstitial spaces.

The wall is thin on purpose:

• endothelium (simple squamous epithelium)

• basement membrane

• a delicate layer of loose connective tissue

Scattered pericapillary cells around them are fibroblasts, macrophages, or undifferentiated smooth muscle cells. There is no thick media and no adventitia like an artery.

check.q: What is the diameter of a capillary, and what three things make its wall?
check.a: 7 to 9 µm; endothelium (simple squamous), basement membrane, and a delicate loose CT layer.

steps.title: How substances cross the wall
steps.text:
Substances cross by diffusion in two ways:

(1) through or between endothelial cells

(2) through fenestrae (windows where cytoplasm is missing and the plasma membrane is thin and porous)

Which path is available depends on the capillary type. Continuous capillaries mostly use path (1). Fenestrated and sinusoidal capillaries add path (2), and sinusoids are leaky enough that even large molecules and cells can move.

check.q: Name the two routes by which substances cross capillary walls.
check.a: Through or between endothelial cells, or through fenestrae.

steps.title: Continuous capillaries
steps.text:
Continuous capillaries are found in many locations, including muscle and nervous tissue.

There are no gaps between endothelial cells and no fenestrae. They are less permeable to large molecules than the other two types. Small lipid-soluble gases still cross the cells themselves; many water-soluble molecules use the narrow clefts between cells.

The lung's alveolar capillaries (next step) are a specialised continuous bed for gas exchange: huge surface, very thin barrier.

check.q: Where are continuous capillaries found, and why are they less leaky?
check.a: Many sites including muscle and nervous tissue; no gaps between endothelial cells and no fenestrae, so large molecules cross poorly.

steps.title: Alveolar capillaries in the lung
steps.text:
In the lung acinus model, find the alveolar capillaries wrapped around air spaces. This is the pulmonary exchange bed: O2 in, CO2 out, across a thin endothelium.

These capillaries are why the pulmonary circuit exists. Blood from the right ventricle must reach this huge, thin network before it can return to the left atrium oxygenated.

check.q: What do alveolar capillaries exchange?
check.a: Gases: oxygen into blood and carbon dioxide out, across a thin endothelial wall.

steps.title: Fenestrated capillaries and the glomerulus
steps.text:
Fenestrated capillaries have endothelial cells with numerous fenestrae where cytoplasm is absent and the plasma membrane is thin and porous. They are highly permeable.

Locations from the lecture: intestinal villi, ciliary process of the eye, choroid plexus, glomeruli of the kidney.

On the nephron model, find the glomerular capillary wall and the podocyte coat (visceral layer) wrapping it. Filtration of blood into the nephron starts here; fenestrae plus the podocyte slits make a filter, not a solid wall.

check.q: Name four places fenestrated capillaries are found.
check.a: Intestinal villi, ciliary process of the eye, choroid plexus, and glomeruli of the kidney.

steps.title: Sinusoidal capillaries in the liver
steps.text:
Sinusoidal capillaries have a large diameter and large fenestrae, with less basement membrane. They are found in endocrine glands and the liver.

On the liver lobule, find sinusoidal endothelial cells lining the channels, Kupffer cells (macrophages sitting in the sinusoids), portal venules bringing blood in, and the central vein taking it out. Blood here is slow and leaky on purpose: hepatocytes take up nutrients; Kupffer cells clean debris.

check.q: How do sinusoidal capillaries differ from continuous ones?
check.a: They have large diameter, large fenestrae and less basement membrane, so they are much more leaky.

steps.title: Match type to job
steps.text:
You can predict the type from what the organ must do.

Need a tight barrier (brain, muscle): continuous.

Need rapid filtration or absorption of fluid and small solutes (glomerulus, gut, choroid plexus): fenestrated.

Need whole proteins or cells to cross, or close contact with lining cells (liver, endocrine glands): sinusoidal.

The histology set labelled capillaries shows real walls; use it to tell a tiny endothelial tube from an arteriole that still has muscle.

check.q: Which capillary type would you expect in a kidney glomerulus, and why?
check.a: Fenestrated: highly permeable windows for filtration of fluid into the nephron.

practice.q: Capillary diameter is…
practice.why: Capillaries are 7 to 9 µm, about the width of a red cell.

practice.q: Continuous capillaries have…
choices: Large fenestrae and little basement membrane
No gaps between endothelial cells and no fenestrae
practice.why: Continuous capillaries lack gaps and fenestrae, so they are less permeable to large molecules.

practice.q: Fenestrated capillaries are found in all of these EXCEPT…
practice.why: Muscle has continuous capillaries. Fenestrated: villi, ciliary process, choroid plexus, glomeruli.

practice.q: Sinusoidal capillaries are typical of…
practice.why: Sinusoids: large diameter, large fenestrae, less basement membrane; liver and endocrine glands.

practice.q: Pericapillary cells may be…
choices: Fibroblasts, macrophages or undifferentiated smooth muscle cells
practice.why: The lecture lists fibroblasts, macrophages or undifferentiated smooth muscle cells.

practice.q: Order capillary types from least to most leaky.
How do substances cross capillary walls?
practice.a: By diffusion through or between endothelial cells, or through fenestrae.

title: Capillary networks, sphincters and anastomoses
summary: Metarterioles, precapillary sphincters, thoroughfare channels, arteriovenous anastomoses and the glomus; which tissues have dense beds.
objectives: Trace blood from arteriole through a capillary network to a venule
Contrast thoroughfare flow with intermittent true-capillary flow
Define arteriovenous anastomoses and a glomus
Say which tissues have more capillary networks and why skin has more thoroughfare channels
takeaways: Arteriole → metarteriole → arterial capillaries → venous capillaries → venule. Precapillary sphincters of metarterioles gate the true capillaries.
Flow through the thoroughfare channel is consistent; flow through arterial capillaries is intermittent.
AV anastomoses skip capillaries (arteriole straight to small vein). A glomus is an AV anastomosis packed with smooth muscle, abundant in sole, palm, terminal phalanges and nail beds, for temperature.
Pathologic AV anastomoses (injury or tumors) can be large and raise venous return enough to cause heart failure.
High-metabolism tissues (lungs, liver, kidneys, skeletal and cardiac muscle) have more networks. Skin uses thoroughfare channels for thermoregulation; muscle beds are for nutrient and waste exchange.

steps.title: From arteriole into the network
steps.text:
Blood does not dump from an arteriole into a random mesh. The usual path is:

arteriole → metarteriole → capillary network

A metarteriole is a short vessel that still has some smooth muscle and that feeds both a direct through-channel and side branches into true capillaries.

The full sequence through the bed is:

arteriole → metarteriole → arterial capillaries → venous capillaries → venule

Follow that order on the diagram before you add sphincters and bypasses.

check.q: Write the path from arteriole to venule through a capillary network.
check.a: Arteriole → metarteriole → arterial capillaries → venous capillaries → venule.

steps.title: Precapillary sphincters: intermittent versus consistent flow
steps.text:
Precapillary sphincters are rings of smooth muscle on the metarteriole at the mouths of true capillaries. They regulate blood flow into the capillary network.

When they open, blood enters the side branches (true capillaries). When they close, blood stays in the through-route.

Two patterns matter for exams:

• Flow through the thoroughfare channel to a venule is consistent (always on).

• Flow through arterial capillaries is intermittent (on and off as sphincters open and close).

check.q: Which flow is consistent and which is intermittent?
check.a: Thoroughfare-channel flow is consistent; flow through arterial capillaries is intermittent.

steps.title: The thoroughfare channel
steps.text:
The thoroughfare channel is the metarteriole continuing straight into a venule. It is the 'highway' through the bed. True capillaries are the 'side streets'.

Tissues can keep some flow even when most sphincters are shut, because the thoroughfare stays open. That matters in skin (next steps) when you need to dump or save heat without always loading every capillary loop.

check.q: What is a thoroughfare channel?
check.a: The direct metarteriole-to-venule route through a capillary bed, with consistent flow.

steps.title: Arteriovenous anastomoses and the glomus
steps.text:
Arteriovenous anastomoses are specialised vascular connections that let blood flow directly from arterioles to small veins, skipping capillaries entirely.

A glomus is an arteriovenous anastomosis with abundant smooth muscle in its walls. Glomera help regulate body temperature by adjusting blood flow through them. They are abundant in the sole of the foot, palm of the hand, terminal phalanges and nail beds.

When a glomus opens, warm arterial blood is shunted toward the skin surface (or the reverse when it closes). That is a temperature tool, not an exchange tool.

check.q: What is a glomus, and where are glomera abundant?
check.a: An AV anastomosis with abundant smooth muscle, for temperature control; sole, palm, terminal phalanges and nail beds.

steps.title: Skin beds: thermoregulation
steps.text:
Tissues with different jobs build different networks. Skin has a thermoregulation function and therefore has more thoroughfare channels. Opening those channels (and AV shunts) sends blood near the surface to lose heat; closing them keeps heat in the core.

On the thin-skin model, find the papillary capillary loops that rise into dermal papillae and the subpapillary plexus that feeds them. The epidermis itself has no vessels; it lives by diffusion from these loops.

check.q: Why does skin have more thoroughfare channels?
check.a: Thermoregulation: they (with AV shunts) adjust how much blood sits near the surface to lose or keep heat.

steps.title: Dense beds, muscle exchange, and pathologic shunts
steps.text:
Tissues with high metabolism have more capillary networks: lungs, liver, kidneys, skeletal muscle, cardiac muscle. In muscle the major function of the bed is nutrient and waste product exchange, not temperature.

Pathologic arteriovenous anastomoses form from injury or tumors and are abnormal. They can be very large and increase venous return enough to lead to heart failure (the right heart is flooded with extra volume that skipped the resistance of a capillary bed).
steps.clinical: A large AV fistula after trauma is a left-to-right volume overload: arterial blood dumps into veins, venous return rises, and the heart can fail.

check.q: Name five high-metabolism tissues with more capillary networks.
check.a: Lungs, liver, kidneys, skeletal muscle and cardiac muscle.

practice.q: Precapillary sphincters regulate flow…
choices: From the vena cava into the atrium
Into the capillary network from metarterioles
practice.why: Sphincters of metarterioles open or close the mouths of true capillaries.

practice.q: Flow through the thoroughfare channel is…
practice.why: Thoroughfare flow is consistent; true arterial-capillary flow is intermittent.

practice.q: An arteriovenous anastomosis lets blood flow…
choices: From arteriole to small vein, skipping capillaries
practice.why: AV anastomoses are direct arteriole-to-small-vein connections.

practice.q: A glomus is…
choices: A fenestrated capillary in the kidney
An AV anastomosis with abundant smooth muscle
practice.why: Glomus = AV anastomosis packed with smooth muscle, used in temperature control.

practice.q: Pathologic AV anastomoses can lead to heart failure because they…
choices: Increase venous return (often are very large)
practice.why: Large abnormal shunts dump arterial blood into veins and raise venous return.

practice.q: Order blood flow through a capillary bed.
Where are glomera abundant?
practice.a: Sole of the foot, palm of the hand, terminal phalanges and nail beds.

practice.q: Which tissues have more capillary networks, and what is the major function of muscle capillary beds?
practice.a: High-metabolism tissues: lungs, liver, kidneys, skeletal and cardiac muscle. In muscle the major function is nutrient and waste exchange.

title: Veins, valves and venous disorders
summary: Venules through large veins, intimal valves in veins greater than 2 mm, and varicose veins, phlebitis and gangrene.
objectives: Classify veins by size and describe each wall
Explain how venous valves are built and where they are more numerous
Describe varicose veins, phlebitis and gangrene as a chain
takeaways: Veins carry blood toward the heart and get larger as they approach it: venules (up to 50 µm) → small veins (0.2 to 0.3 mm) → medium (1 mm to 1 cm) → large veins.
Valves: all veins greater than 2 mm; two overlapping intimal flaps; more in lower than upper extremities.
Varicose veins: incompetent lower-limb valves, raised venous pressure and edema, possible hemorrhoids, stagnant flow and clots; causes include genetics, pregnancy, standing.
Phlebitis = inflammation of veins; severe cases leave large stagnant areas. Prolonged phlebitis can cause gangrene (tissue death from loss of blood supply).

steps.title: Veins: toward the heart, and larger as they go
steps.text:
Veins carry blood toward the heart. Unlike arteries, the vessels get larger as they approach the heart.

Classifications:

• venules

• small veins

• medium or large veins

Pressure is low, so the wall is thinner than a matching artery, the lumen is wider (often collapsed on a slide), and many veins have valves. The venae cavae in the atlas are large veins emptying into the right atrium.

check.q: Which way do veins carry blood, and what happens to their size toward the heart?
check.a: Toward the heart; they get larger as they approach it.

steps.title: Venules
steps.text:
Venules have a diameter up to 50 µm. They drain the capillary network.

Their wall is endothelial cells and basement membrane with a few smooth muscle cells. As venule diameter increases, the proportion of smooth muscle increases. They pass blood to small veins.

Think of a venule as a capillary that has started to grow a little muscle, not yet a named vein.

check.q: What is the diameter of venules, and what do they drain?
check.a: Up to 50 µm; they drain the capillary network.

steps.title: Small and medium veins
steps.text:
Small veins (0.2 to 0.3 mm): smooth muscle cells now form a continuous layer. The tunica adventitia is collagenous CT. They pass blood to medium veins.

Medium veins (1 mm to 1 cm): thin tunica intima, circular smooth muscle in the tunica media, and the tunica externa is predominant. They pass blood to large veins.

On the vein-wall model the media is a thin muscle coat compared with a muscular artery, and the adventitia is relatively thick.

check.q: Which layer is predominant in medium veins?
check.a: The tunica externa (adventitia).

steps.title: Large veins
steps.text:
Large veins (the venae cavae are the examples you can see) have:

• a thin tunica intima of endothelial cells, a thin CT layer and scattered elastic fibers

• a tunica media with circularly arranged smooth muscle cells

• a tunica externa that is the predominant layer

They are capacitance vessels: a wide lumen at low pressure. That idea returns as venous compliance (about 24 times that of arteries) and as the blood reservoir in Table 21.13.

check.q: In a large vein, which tunic is predominant?
check.a: Tunica externa.

steps.title: Valves: folds of intima in veins greater than 2 mm
steps.text:
Valves are found in all veins greater than 2 mm in diameter. They are folds of intima that form two overlapping flaps.

There are more valves in veins of the lower extremities than in veins of the upper extremities, because those veins fight gravity.

On the model, find the venous valve cusps projecting into the lumen, lined by endothelium. Blood can push the flaps open toward the heart and they close if blood tries to fall back.
steps.pitfall: Arteries do not have these valves. Do not 'find a valve' on an artery slide.

check.q: How are venous valves built, and in which veins are they found?
check.a: Two overlapping flaps that are folds of intima, in all veins greater than 2 mm; more in the lower limbs.

steps.title: Varicose veins, phlebitis and gangrene
steps.text:
Varicose veins: valves of the lower limbs become incompetent (too much stretch). Venous pressure rises and edema forms in the lower limbs; hemorrhoids are possible. Stagnant blood flow can lead to clots. Causes: genetics, pregnancy, standing for long periods.

Phlebitis: inflammation of veins. If severe, it can leave large areas of stagnant blood.

Gangrene: tissue death from loss of blood supply. It can result from prolonged phlebitis.

The chain to remember: stretch and failed valves → stasis → inflammation and clot → if perfusion is lost, tissue death.
steps.clinical: Standing still for hours lets blood pool below the heart. Muscle movement (next lessons) and intact valves are what normally prevent that pool from stretching the walls.

check.q: What makes a vein varicose, and what three complications does the lecture list?
check.a: Incompetent (overstretched) lower-limb valves. Raised pressure and edema (possible hemorrhoids), clots from stagnant flow; phlebitis can follow, and prolonged phlebitis can cause gangrene.

practice.q: Venules are up to…
practice.why: Venules drain capillaries and are up to 50 µm wide.

practice.q: Small veins are about…
practice.why: Small veins are 0.2 to 0.3 mm, with a continuous smooth-muscle layer.

practice.q: Valves are found in…
choices: All veins greater than 2 mm in diameter
practice.why: Intimal valves sit in veins > 2 mm; more of them in the lower limbs.

practice.q: Venous valves are…
choices: Folds of intima forming two overlapping flaps
practice.why: Valves are two overlapping intimal flaps.

practice.q: Gangrene in this lecture is…
choices: Tissue death from loss of blood supply, which can follow prolonged phlebitis
A valve in a large vein
practice.why: Gangrene is tissue death from lost supply; prolonged phlebitis can cause it.

practice.q: Causes of varicose veins include…
choices: Genetics, pregnancy and standing for long periods
practice.why: The lecture lists genetics, pregnancy and standing.

practice.q: Order veins from smallest to largest class.
Why are there more valves in lower-extremity veins than in upper-extremity veins?
practice.a: Lower-limb veins fight gravity; more valves stop backflow.

title: Portal systems, vasa vasorum and vessel nerves
summary: The three human portal systems, nutrient vessels of large walls, and sympathetic versus parasympathetic innervation of vessels.
objectives: Define a portal vein and name the three human portal systems
Trace the idea of the hepatic, hypothalamohypophyseal and renal nephron portals
Explain vasa vasorum
Describe neural innervation of blood vessels, including baroreceptor fibers
takeaways: A portal vein begins in a primary capillary network and runs to a second capillary network with no heart in between.
Humans: hepatic portal (GI capillaries → liver sinusoids), hypothalamohypophyseal (hypothalamus → anterior pituitary), renal nephron portal (inside urine-forming kidney structures).
Vasa vasorum: vessels > 1 mm, from the exterior into externa and media.

Unmyelinated sympathetic plexuses in adventitia (especially small arteries and arterioles) cause vasoconstriction. Penis and clitoris: parasympathetic vasodilation. A few myelinated sensory fibers are baroreceptors (stretch and change in BP).

steps.title: What a portal system is
steps.text:
Usually blood goes through one capillary bed per circuit, then veins, then the heart. A portal vein is different: it begins in a primary capillary network and extends to a secondary capillary network without a pumping mechanism in between.

Humans have three portal systems. The hepatic one is asked about most. The other two are short and local: brain and kidney.

check.q: Define a portal vein.
check.a: A vein that begins in one capillary network and runs to a second capillary network with no heart (no pump) in between.

steps.title: Hepatic portal system
steps.text:
Hepatic portal veins carry nutrient-rich blood from GI capillaries to the liver, where they dilate and become sinusoidal capillaries.

That second bed lets the liver process absorbed nutrients and clean the blood before it reaches the heart and the rest of the body. On the lobule model, portal venules feed sinusoids (endothelium plus Kupffer cells) that drain to the central vein, then toward hepatic veins and the inferior vena cava.

The lab diagram shows the named tributaries; this lecture only needs the idea: gut capillaries → portal vein → liver sinusoids.

check.q: What does the hepatic portal system connect?
check.a: GI (digestive) capillaries to liver sinusoidal capillaries, carrying nutrient-rich blood with no heart in between.

steps.title: Hypothalamohypophyseal portal system
steps.text:
The hypothalamohypophyseal portal system runs between the hypothalamus and the anterior pituitary gland. Releasing and inhibiting hormones travel this short portal route so they hit the anterior pituitary in high concentration instead of being diluted in the whole bloodstream.

The atlas shows the hypothalamus and the neurohypophysis (posterior pituitary) as nearby landmarks. The portal veins themselves go to the anterior lobe, which is not a separate atlas piece here; use the hypothalamus as the start point.
steps.pitfall: The neurohypophysis stores hypothalamic hormones delivered by axons, not by this portal system. The portal system is hypothalamus → anterior pituitary.

check.q: The hypothalamohypophyseal portal system links which two regions?
check.a: The hypothalamus and the anterior pituitary gland.

steps.title: Renal nephron portal system
steps.text:
The third human portal system is the renal nephron portal system, within the urine-forming structures of the kidneys.

Blood is filtered in the glomerular capillaries, then goes through an efferent arteriole into a second capillary bed (peritubular capillaries and vasa recta) around the tubules. Two beds, one nephron, no heart in between: that is a portal arrangement.

Find the kidney in the atlas, then remember the glomerulus you already saw on the nephron model.

check.q: Where is the renal nephron portal system?
check.a: Within the urine-forming structures of the kidneys (glomerulus then a second capillary bed around the tubules).

steps.title: Vasa vasorum, revisited as a system
steps.text:
You saw vasa vasorum in the wall. The definition to memorise:

Small vessels that supply nutrients to arteries and veins greater than 1 mm, whose diameter is too large for diffusion of nutrients from the lumen. They penetrate from the exterior and form a capillary network in the tunica externa and tunica media.

Without them the outer wall of the aorta would starve. They are not a portal system; they are the wall's own systemic supply.

check.q: Which vessels have vasa vasorum, and from which direction do they enter?
check.a: Arteries and veins greater than 1 mm; they penetrate from the exterior into externa and media.

steps.title: Neural innervation of blood vessels
steps.text:
Unmyelinated sympathetic nerve fibers form plexuses in the tunica adventitia. Small arteries and arterioles are the most innervated. Sympathetic activity causes vasoconstriction.

Vessels of the penis and clitoris are innervated by parasympathetic fibers, which cause vasodilation.

A few myelinated sensory fibers innervate certain vessels and act as baroreceptors: they monitor stretch and change in blood pressure. That sensory story becomes the baroreceptor reflex in the short-term BP lesson. The vagus nerve is one of the cranial routes involved.

check.q: What do sympathetic fibers to small arteries and arterioles cause, and what do baroreceptor fibers monitor?
check.a: Vasoconstriction; stretch and change in blood pressure.

practice.q: A portal vein runs…
choices: From an artery to a vein with a heart in between
From a primary capillary network to a secondary capillary network with no pump in between
From the aorta to the vena cava directly
practice.why: Portal: capillary bed → vein → second capillary bed, no heart between.

practice.q: How many portal systems do humans have?
practice.why: Hepatic, hypothalamohypophyseal, and renal nephron.

practice.q: Hepatic portal blood is…
choices: Nutrient-rich from GI capillaries, becoming sinusoids in the liver
practice.why: GI capillaries → hepatic portal veins → liver sinusoids.

practice.q: The hypothalamohypophyseal portal system is between…
practice.why: It links hypothalamus to anterior pituitary.

practice.q: Sympathetic innervation of small arteries and arterioles causes…
practice.why: Unmyelinated sympathetic plexuses in adventitia vasoconstrict; small arteries and arterioles are most innervated.

practice.q: Parasympathetic vasodilation is described for vessels of the…
practice.why: The lecture names penis and clitoris as parasympathetic vasodilator targets.

practice.q: Order the hepatic portal idea from gut to heart.
What do myelinated sensory fibers on certain vessels act as?
practice.a: Baroreceptors that monitor stretch and change in blood pressure.

title: Laminar flow, turbulent flow and measuring blood pressure
summary: Streamlined versus interrupted flow, Korotkoff sounds, and the auscultatory cuff on the brachial artery.
objectives: Contrast laminar and turbulent flow
Define blood pressure
Describe the auscultatory method and Korotkoff sounds
Say which pressure is systolic and which is diastolic
takeaways: Laminar: smooth equal-diameter vessel; concentric rings, outermost slowest, center fastest.
Turbulent: flow exceeds critical velocity, or constriction, sharp turn, or rough surface; contributes to heart sounds; not normal in arteries (suggests constriction; raises thrombosis risk).
BP = force of blood against vessel walls; blood moves because of that pressure.
Cuff above the elbow, stethoscope on the brachial artery. First Korotkoff sound = systolic. Sound disappears when laminar flow returns = diastolic.

steps.title: Hemodynamics is flow, resistance and pressure
steps.text:
The second half of the chapter is hemodynamics: the interrelationships among flow, resistance and pressure. Control mechanisms that regulate blood pressure and blood flow are critical to the circulatory system.

Before equations, you need two pictures of how blood actually moves in a tube, and how we listen to that motion with a cuff.

check.q: Hemodynamics relates which three quantities?
check.a: Flow, resistance and pressure.

steps.title: Laminar flow
steps.text:
Laminar flow is streamlined. It happens when the interior of the blood vessel is smooth and of equal diameter along its length.

Fluids behave as if they were made of concentric rings: the outermost layer flows slowest (rubbing the wall) and the center flows fastest.

This is the quiet, normal pattern in a healthy artery. No extra noise, no extra mixing.

check.q: In laminar flow, which part of the stream is fastest?
check.a: The center; the outermost ring, against the wall, is slowest.

steps.title: Turbulent flow
steps.text:
Turbulent flow is interrupted. It happens when the rate of flow exceeds critical velocity, or when fluid passes a constriction, a sharp turn, or a rough surface.

Turbulence is partly responsible for heart sounds. Turbulence sounds are not normal in arteries; they probably mean some constriction, and turbulence increases the probability of thrombosis (clotting).

We exploit a brief, controlled turbulence when we measure blood pressure: the cuff creates a constriction on purpose.
steps.clinical: A bruit over an artery is turbulent flow from narrowing. It is not a normal arterial sound.

check.q: Name three situations that cause turbulent flow, and one risk it raises in arteries.
check.a: Flow above critical velocity; a constriction, sharp turn or rough surface. It increases the chance of thrombosis. It is not a normal arterial sound.

steps.title: Blood pressure is a force on the wall
steps.text:
Blood pressure is the measure of force exerted by blood against blood vessel walls. Blood moves through vessels because of blood pressure (always from higher to lower pressure).

It can be measured directly with a cannula in a vessel, or indirectly by the auscultatory method: a sphygmomanometer and a stethoscope to listen for Korotkoff sounds, which are turbulent flow in arteries as pressure is released from the cuff.

check.q: What is blood pressure, and what are Korotkoff sounds?
check.a: Force of blood against vessel walls. Korotkoff sounds are turbulent flow heard as cuff pressure is released.

steps.title: The cuff on the brachial artery
steps.text:
The blood-pressure cuff, connected to a sphygmomanometer, is wrapped around the arm just above the elbow. The stethoscope is placed over the brachial artery.

The cuff is inflated until the brachial artery is completely collapsed (no sounds). Pressure is then lowered gradually. Blood starts to flow through the constricted area during systole: flow is turbulent and produces vibrations heard as Korotkoff sounds.

Find the brachial artery in the atlas in the anterior arm, where a cuff would sit.

check.q: Where is the cuff placed, and over which artery is the stethoscope placed?
check.a: Cuff around the arm just above the elbow; stethoscope over the brachial artery.

steps.title: First sound systolic, silence diastolic
steps.text:
The pressure at which a Korotkoff sound is first heard is systolic pressure.

As cuff pressure falls, the sounds change tone and loudness. When pressure has dropped enough that continuous laminar blood flow is reestablished, the sound disappears. That pressure is diastolic pressure.

So: silence (artery shut) → tapping (systolic, turbulence) → changing sounds → silence again (laminar, diastolic). You are listening to the shift from no flow, to turbulent flow, to laminar flow.
steps.pitfall: Diastolic is not 'the last loud sound.' It is the pressure where sound disappears because laminar flow has returned.

check.q: What is systolic pressure and what is diastolic pressure in the auscultatory method?
check.a: Systolic: pressure at the first Korotkoff sound. Diastolic: pressure when sound disappears because continuous laminar flow is back.

practice.q: In laminar flow the fastest blood is…
choices: In the center of the vessel
practice.why: Concentric rings: outermost slowest, center fastest.

practice.q: Turbulence sounds in arteries are…
choices: How diastolic pressure is defined in the heart
practice.why: Arterial turbulence is not normal; it likely means constriction and raises thrombosis risk.

practice.q: Korotkoff sounds are…
choices: Turbulent flow in arteries as cuff pressure is released
practice.why: They are turbulence heard while the cuff still narrows the artery.

practice.q: The auscultatory method uses a stethoscope over the…
practice.why: Cuff above the elbow; listen over the brachial artery.

practice.q: Diastolic pressure is the cuff pressure at which…
choices: Sound disappears as laminar flow returns
practice.why: When continuous laminar flow is reestablished, Korotkoff sounds vanish: that is diastolic.

practice.q: Order the auscultatory steps.
items: Inflate cuff until the brachial artery is collapsed (silence)
Lower pressure until the first Korotkoff sound (systolic)
Sounds change as the constriction eases
Sounds disappear when laminar flow returns (diastolic)

practice.q: Define blood pressure.
practice.a: The force exerted by blood against blood vessel walls; it is why blood moves through vessels.

practice.q: Name three causes of turbulent flow.
practice.a: Flow exceeding critical velocity; passing a constriction, a sharp turn, or a rough surface.

practice.q: Laminar flow requires a vessel interior that is…
choices: Smooth and of equal diameter along its length
practice.why: Streamlined flow needs a smooth, even-diameter lumen.

title: Flow equals ΔP over R, Laplace, and venous compliance
summary: F = ΔP/R, viscosity and hematocrit, Laplace and aneurysms, critical closing pressure, veins 24 times as compliant as arteries, and Table 21.13 volumes.
objectives: Write F = ΔP/R and say what raises or lowers flow
Relate viscosity and hematocrit to workload on the heart
State Laplace's law and relate it to aneurysms and critical closing pressure
Give venous versus arterial compliance and the Table 21.13 volume percents
takeaways: Flow = (P1 − P2)/R = ΔP/R. Flow is directly proportional to the pressure drop and inversely proportional to resistance. Viscosity and vessel diameter matter most for R; length is less critical.
Constriction raises R and lowers flow. In exercise aortic pressure rises and muscle capillaries widen, so aortic flow can go from 5 L/min to 25 L/min.
Viscosity: as hematocrit rises, viscosity rises logarithmically; dehydration or excess RBCs raise viscosity and heart workload.

Laplace: F = D × P. Bigger diameter or higher pressure means more wall force; a weak spot bulges (aneurysm). Critical closing pressure: the pressure at which a vessel collapses and flow stops (a shock concern).
Veins are about 24 times as compliant as arteries (blood reservoir). Systemic veins hold 64% of blood volume; systemic vessels 84%; pulmonary 9%; heart 7%.

steps.title: Blood flow is a volume per time, and F = ΔP/R
steps.text:
Flow through a tube is the volume that passes a specific point per unit of time. Cardiac output at rest is about 5 L/min, so flow through the aorta is 5 L/min.

The lecture equation is:

F = (P1 − P2)/R or F = ΔP / R

P1 and P2 are pressures at two points along the vessel. R is resistance. Blood always flows from higher to lower pressure. Flow is directly proportional to ΔP and inversely proportional to R.

Viscosity and vessel diameter are the most important factors in resistance. Length of the vessel is not as critical for R.

check.q: Write the flow equation and name the two most important resistance factors.
check.a: F = ΔP/R. Viscosity and vessel diameter matter most for R; length is less critical.

steps.title: Poiseuille's law in words: diameter changes flow
steps.text:
In the idealized Poiseuille model, R = 8ηL/(πr⁴) and Q = ΔP/R. Increasing viscosity or length increases resistance; increasing radius greatly reduces it. Halving radius raises resistance sixteenfold at fixed viscosity and length.

During exercise, dilation of upstream resistance vessels and recruitment of perfused capillaries increase skeletal-muscle flow. Capillaries are not miniature muscular arterioles. Aortic flow can rise from about 5 L/min toward 25 L/min in the course example.

check.q: At fixed pressure gradient, viscosity and length, what does halving radius do to idealized flow?
check.a: Resistance increases sixteenfold and flow falls to one sixteenth.

steps.title: Viscosity and hematocrit
steps.text:
Viscosity is a measure of a liquid's resistance to flow. As viscosity rises, the pressure required to make it flow rises.

Blood viscosity is influenced largely by hematocrit (the fraction that is red cells). As hematocrit rises, viscosity rises logarithmically (not just linearly: a little extra hematocrit costs a lot of extra stickiness at the high end).

Dehydration and/or uncontrolled production of RBCs can raise viscosity and increase workload on the heart.
steps.clinical: Polycythemia or severe dehydration makes blood 'thicker,' so the same cardiac output needs more pressure.

check.q: What largely determines blood viscosity, and why does that matter to the heart?
check.a: Hematocrit; as it rises, viscosity rises logarithmically and the heart must work harder to move the blood.

steps.title: Critical closing pressure and Laplace's law
steps.text:
Critical closing pressure is the pressure at which a blood vessel collapses and blood flow stops. That is a concern during circulatory shock, when pressure can fall below the closing point of many small vessels.

Laplace's law: the force acting on a blood vessel wall is proportional to the diameter of the vessel times blood pressure.

F = D × P

As diameter increases, force on the wall increases. A weakened part of a vessel wall bulges out: an aneurysm. Once it bulges, D is even larger, so F is even larger: a vicious circle.
steps.clinical: An aortic aneurysm is Laplace in real life: the bigger the bulge, the greater the wall force at the same pressure.

check.q: State Laplace's law and define an aneurysm in those terms.
check.a: F = D × P. A weakened wall bulges; the larger diameter then raises wall force further.

steps.title: Vascular compliance: veins as a reservoir
steps.text:
Compliance is the tendency for blood-vessel volume to increase as blood pressure increases. The more easily the wall stretches, the greater the compliance.

The venous system has a large compliance, about 24 times greater than that of arteries. That is why veins act as a blood reservoir: a small pressure change stores or releases a large volume.

check.q: How does venous compliance compare with arterial compliance, and what is the functional result?
check.a: About 24 times greater; veins act as a blood reservoir.

steps.title: Table 21.13: where the blood sits
steps.text:
Memorize the percents of total blood volume.

VesselsTotal blood volume (%)
Systemic veins (large 39 + small 25)64
Systemic arteries (large 8 + small 5 + arterioles 2)15
Systemic capillaries5
Total in systemic vessels84
Pulmonary vessels9
Heart7
Total100

Almost two-thirds of the blood is in systemic veins. That matches 24× compliance: the reservoir is venous.

check.q: What percent of blood volume is in systemic veins, and what percent in the heart?
check.a: 64% in systemic veins; 7% in the heart.

practice.q: Flow equals…
practice.why: F = ΔP/R: flow rises with the pressure drop and falls as resistance rises.

practice.q: The most important resistance factors are…
practice.why: Viscosity and diameter matter most; length is less critical.

practice.q: In exercise, aortic flow can rise from about…
practice.why: Greater aortic pressure plus dilated muscle vessels: 5 to 25 L/min.

practice.q: Laplace's law is…
practice.why: Wall force is proportional to diameter times pressure.

practice.q: Venous compliance compared with arterial is about…
practice.why: Veins are ~24× as compliant and act as a reservoir.

practice.q: Systemic veins hold about what percent of blood volume?
practice.why: Table 21.13: veins 64% (large 39 + small 25).

practice.q: Critical closing pressure is…
choices: The pressure at which a vessel collapses and flow stops
practice.why: Below that pressure the vessel collapses; a concern in shock.

practice.q: Order Table 21.13 compartments from largest share of blood volume to smallest.
Why does a rising hematocrit burden the heart?
practice.a: Viscosity rises logarithmically with hematocrit, so more pressure (more work) is needed to keep flow.

practice.q: Using Laplace, why does an aneurysm tend to worsen?
practice.a: A bulge raises diameter, so F = D × P increases, stretching the weak wall further.

title: Cross-sectional area, pressure drop, pulse and BP classes
summary: Aorta 5 cm² versus capillaries 2500 cm², greatest pressure drop in arterioles, pulse pressure, radial pulse, and Table 21.14 adult classes.
objectives: Relate total cross-sectional area to velocity
Say where pressure falls most and why capillaries have no large pressure swings
Define pulse pressure and where the radial pulse is taken
Recite Table 21.14 adult blood-pressure classes
takeaways: As vessel diameter falls, total cross-sectional area rises and velocity falls. Aorta about 5 cm²; all capillaries about 2500 cm² (stream in a gorge versus a broad plain).
BP averages about 100 mm Hg in the aorta and drops to 0 mm Hg at the right atrium. Greatest drop is in the arterioles. No large fluctuations in capillaries or veins.
Pulse pressure = systolic − diastolic. It rises when stroke volume rises or compliance falls (compliance falls with age/arteriosclerosis). Radial pulse at the carpus is the usual HR site.
Table 21.14: Normal <120 and <80; Elevated 120–129 and <80; Stage 1 130–139 or 80–89; Stage 2 ≥140 or ≥90; Hypertensive crisis >180 and/or >120.

steps.title: Total area goes up, so speed goes down
steps.text:
As the diameter of individual vessels falls, the total cross-sectional area of all of them together rises, and the velocity of blood flow falls.

The aorta has a cross-sectional area of about 5 cm2. The total cross-sectional area of all capillaries is about 2500 cm2.

The lecture's picture: a stream that flows rapidly through a narrow gorge (aorta) but slowly through a broad plain (capillary bed). Slow flow in capillaries is what gives time for exchange.

check.q: Give the cross-sectional areas of the aorta and of all capillaries together.
check.a: Aorta about 5 cm²; all capillaries about 2500 cm². Velocity is high in the aorta and lowest in capillaries.

steps.title: Pressure from 100 mm Hg to zero
steps.text:
Blood pressure averages about 100 mm Hg in the aorta and drops to 0 mm Hg at the right atrium. That whole drop is what drives systemic flow (ΔP in F = ΔP/R).

Resistance to flow rises as total cross-sectional area rises, but the greatest drop in pressure is in the arterioles (they can constrict, and they are the last high-resistance stop before the huge capillary area).

There are no large fluctuations in capillaries or veins: the pulse has been damped out. Muscular arteries and arterioles can still constrict or dilate in response to autonomic and hormonal stimulation.

check.q: Where is the greatest pressure drop, and what are the aortic and right-atrial pressures given?
check.a: Greatest drop in the arterioles. About 100 mm Hg in the aorta, 0 mm Hg at the right atrium.

steps.title: Velocity follows the same map
steps.text:
Blood pressure falls as you get farther from the heart. Greater resistance (smaller individual diameters) also affects how fast pressure changes along the tree.

Blood moves fastest in the aorta and large arteries and slowest in the capillaries. After the capillaries, veins have a smaller total area than the capillary bed, so velocity rises again on the way back, but pressure stays low.

check.q: Where is blood fastest and where is it slowest?
check.a: Fastest in the aorta and large arteries; slowest in the capillaries.

steps.title: Pulse pressure
steps.text:
Pulse pressure is the difference between systolic and diastolic pressures.

It increases when stroke volume increases or when vascular compliance decreases. Compliance tends to decrease with age (arteriosclerosis), so pulse pressure rises.

The pulse can be used to take heart rate and rhythmicity. The most frequent site is in the carpus with the radial artery (radial pulse).

check.q: Define pulse pressure and name the usual pulse site.
check.a: Systolic minus diastolic pressure. The radial artery at the wrist (carpus) is the most frequent site.

steps.title: Table 21.14: adult blood-pressure classes
steps.text:
These ACC/AHA adult numbers are a table to memorise. Systolic and diastolic are judged together with 'and' or 'or' as written.

Systolic (mm Hg)Diastolic (mm Hg)
Normal<120and<80
Elevated120 to 129and<80
Stage 1 hypertension130 to 139or80 to 89
Stage 2 hypertension≥140or≥90
Hypertensive crisis>180and/or>120

Later the lecture also uses older cutoffs for hypo- and hypertension as clinical labels. Learn both; this table is the classification chart.

check.q: What values are 'normal' and what values are a hypertensive crisis?
check.a: Normal: systolic <120 and diastolic <80. Crisis: systolic >180 and/or diastolic >120.

steps.title: Putting area, pressure and pulse together
steps.text:
Stand at the aorta: small total area, high velocity, about 100 mm Hg mean, a clear pulse (systolic minus diastolic).

Walk to the arterioles: biggest pressure drop, still some ability to change R.

Arrive at capillaries: huge total area (2500 cm²), slowest flow, almost no pulse.

Feel the radial artery: you are still on a muscular artery, so a pulse remains. That pulse is the leftover of the aortic pressure swing, reduced by compliance of the arterial tree.

check.q: Why is there little pressure fluctuation in capillaries and veins?
check.a: The pulse has been damped; the greatest pressure drop has already occurred in the arterioles.

practice.q: Total capillary cross-sectional area is about…
practice.why: All capillaries together ≈ 2500 cm² versus aorta ≈ 5 cm².

practice.q: The greatest drop in blood pressure occurs in the…
practice.why: Arterioles are the main resistance stop; the lecture says the greatest drop is there.

practice.q: Pulse pressure is…
practice.why: Pulse pressure = systolic − diastolic.

practice.q: Pulse pressure increases when…
choices: Stroke volume falls and compliance rises
Stroke volume rises or vascular compliance falls
The person is in laminar flow only
practice.why: ↑ SV or ↓ compliance (as in arteriosclerosis with age) widens pulse pressure.

practice.q: Stage 2 hypertension is…
practice.why: Table 21.14: Stage 2 is systolic ≥140 or diastolic ≥90.

practice.q: The most frequent pulse site is the…
practice.why: Radial pulse at the wrist is the usual site for rate and rhythmicity.

practice.q: Order Table 21.14 classes from lowest pressures to crisis.
Average BP in the aorta versus at the right atrium?
practice.a: About 100 mm Hg in the aorta, 0 mm Hg at the right atrium.

practice.q: Why is capillary flow slow?
practice.a: Total cross-sectional area is huge (~2500 cm²), so velocity falls, like a stream spreading over a broad plain.

title: Capillary exchange and venous return
summary: Lipid- versus water-soluble diffusion, 30 L out / 27 L back / 3 L lymph, muscular respiratory and sympathetic pumps, and gravity.
objectives: Contrast lipid-soluble and water-soluble capillary crossing
Give the 30 / 27 / 3 litre figures and what happens to the leftover
Name the muscular, respiratory and sympathetic pumps
Explain how standing and gravity affect lower-limb filtration
takeaways: Diffusion is the main exchange. Lipid-soluble (O2, CO2, steroids, fatty acids) through membranes; water-soluble (glucose, amino acids) through clefts or fenestrae.
Fluid out at the arterial end, most back in at the venous end. 30 L/day out, 27 L back, 3 L picked up by lymphatics.
Venous return rises with blood volume, venous tone, compression of veins, and arteriole dilation. Pumps: muscular (valves stop backflow), respiratory, sympathetic venoconstriction (venous tone).

Standing: hydrostatic pressure raises BP below the heart and lowers it above. About 15 to 20% of blood volume can filter in the lower limbs in 15 minutes of standing still → edema. Muscle movement fixes it.

steps.title: Diffusion is the main way things cross
steps.text:
Diffusion is the most important means of exchange across capillaries.

Lipid-soluble substances cross by diffusing through plasma membranes: O2, CO2, steroid hormones, fatty acids.

Water-soluble substances diffuse through intercellular spaces or through fenestrations: glucose and amino acids.

That is the same split you already used for continuous versus fenestrated walls, now named by the solute.

check.q: Give two lipid-soluble and two water-soluble examples, and the path each uses.
check.a: Lipid-soluble (O₂, CO₂, steroids, fatty acids) through membranes. Water-soluble (glucose, amino acids) through clefts or fenestrae.

steps.title: Fluid out at the arterial end, in at the venous end
steps.text:
Blood pressure, capillary permeability and osmosis affect movement of fluid.

Fluid moves out of capillaries at the arterial end (blood pressure is higher there than the osmotic pull inward).

Most fluid returns to capillaries at the venous end (blood pressure has fallen; osmotic pull from plasma proteins now wins).

Whatever remains in the tissues is picked up by the lymphatic system and returned to venous circulation. That leftover is not a rounding error; it is tomorrow's lymph chapter, but the numbers are in this lecture.

check.q: Where does fluid leave capillaries and where does most of it return?
check.a: Out at the arterial end; most returns at the venous end; leftover goes to lymphatics.

steps.title: Thirty, twenty-seven, three
steps.text:
Each day about 30 L of fluid leaves capillaries into interstitial fluid. About 27 L returns into the venous ends. The remaining 3 L is picked up as lymph.

If lymphatics fail, that 3 L stays in the tissue: edema. If venous pressure stays high (failed valves, standing still), more than 30 L may leave and the 27 L return cannot keep up.

check.q: Give the daily volumes out of capillaries, back in, and into lymph.
check.a: 30 L out, 27 L back into capillaries, 3 L into lymphatics.

steps.title: Venous return (preload) and the three pumps
steps.text:
Venous return is preload: blood coming back to the heart. It increases with an increase in blood volume, venous tone, compression of veins, or arteriole dilation.

Muscular pump: contraction of skeletal muscles 'milks' blood toward the heart; valves prevent backflow.

Respiratory pump: pressure changes during breathing move blood toward the heart by squeezing abdominal veins as thoracic veins expand.

Sympathetic venoconstriction: under sympathetic control, smooth muscle constricts, pushing blood toward the heart (venous tone).

check.q: Name the three pumps that raise venous return.
check.a: Muscular pump (with valves), respiratory pump, and sympathetic venoconstriction (venous tone).

steps.title: Gravity, standing still, and edema
steps.text:
In a standing position, hydrostatic pressure caused by gravity increases blood pressure below the heart and decreases it above the heart.

About 15 to 20% of total blood volume can pass through the walls of capillaries of the lower limbs during 15 minutes of standing still, resulting in edema.

Muscular movement improves venous return (the muscular pump), so walking prevents that pool. This is the same physics as varicose veins: still standing, high venous pressure, fluid out.

check.q: What happens to lower-limb capillary filtration if you stand still for 15 minutes?
check.a: About 15 to 20% of blood volume can filter into the lower limbs, causing edema. Muscle movement improves venous return and prevents it.

steps.title: Local, nervous and hormonal hints (preview)
steps.text:
The lecture's bridge into control:

• Local control: in most tissues, flow is proportional to metabolic needs.

• Nervous system: routes blood flow and maintains BP.

• Hormonal control: sympathetic action potentials stimulate epinephrine and norepinephrine.

Those ideas become MAP, baroreceptors and RAAS in the next lessons. For now, hold that venous return sets stroke volume (preload), so anything that raises venous return can raise cardiac output if the heart can pump it.

check.q: Name four things whose increase raises venous return.
check.a: Blood volume, venous tone, compression of veins, and arteriole dilation.

practice.q: Lipid-soluble substances such as O₂ and CO₂ cross capillaries by…
practice.why: Lipid-soluble solutes (O₂, CO₂, steroids, fatty acids) diffuse through membranes.

practice.q: Glucose and amino acids mainly cross by…
practice.why: Water-soluble solutes use clefts or fenestrae.

practice.q: Daily capillary fluid movement is about…
choices: 3 L out, 30 L back, 27 L lymph
30 L out, 27 L back, 3 L lymph
27 L out, 3 L back, 30 L lymph
Equal in and out with no lymph
practice.why: 30 L out, 27 L return, 3 L to lymphatics.

practice.q: The respiratory pump works by…
choices: Closing all valves in the neck
Squeezing abdominal veins as thoracic veins expand during breathing
practice.why: Breathing pressure changes milk blood toward the heart.

practice.q: Standing still for 15 minutes can move about how much of blood volume into lower-limb tissues?
practice.why: Hydrostatic pressure filters ~15–20% of blood volume in 15 minutes of standing still → edema.

practice.q: Order capillary fluid handling in a day.
items: Fluid leaves at the arterial end
Most fluid re-enters at the venous end

practice.q: Name the three venous-return pumps.
practice.a: Muscular pump (valves prevent backflow), respiratory pump, sympathetic venoconstriction (venous tone).

practice.q: What three factors affect fluid movement at capillaries besides solute type?
practice.a: Blood pressure, capillary permeability and osmosis.

title: MAP and short-term blood-pressure reflexes
summary: MAP = HR × SV × PR, the daily baroreceptor reflex, adrenal medullary, chemoreceptor and CNS ischemic responses.
objectives: Define MAP and write MAP = CO × PR = HR × SV × PR
Give typical MAP values across life
Explain the baroreceptor reflex as the main daily control
Contrast adrenal medullary, chemoreceptor and CNS ischemic responses
takeaways: MAP is slightly less than the average of systolic and diastolic because diastole lasts longer. ~70 mm Hg at birth, 100 from adolescence to middle age, 110 in healthy older people.
MAP = CO × PR = HR × SV × PR. Raise any of the three and MAP rises. SV depends on venous return (EDV); HR from medullary centers; R mostly from vessel diameter.
Baroreceptor reflex (ΔBP changes PR, HR and SV) is the most important day-to-day control. Sensors in stretching aortic and carotid walls.

Adrenal medulla: epinephrine and norepinephrine in exercise, emergencies, or a fall in BP. Chemoreceptors: O2, CO2, pH (high altitude, high CO2, low pH). CNS ischemic response: last-ditch vasoconstriction when the medulla itself is underperfused.

steps.title: Mean arterial pressure
steps.text:
MAP is slightly less than the average of systolic and diastolic pressures because diastole lasts longer than systole.

Across a lifetime:

• about 70 mm Hg at birth

• about 100 mm Hg from adolescence to middle age

• about 110 mm Hg in healthy older individuals

If BP is too high, heart and vessels may be damaged. If the system cannot keep a normal BP, flow throughout the body is inadequate: circulatory shock, which can kill. That is why MAP is defended so aggressively.

check.q: Why is MAP a little less than (systolic + diastolic)/2, and what is MAP from adolescence to middle age?
check.a: Diastole lasts longer than systole. About 100 mm Hg from adolescence to middle age.

steps.title: MAP = HR × SV × PR
steps.text:
MAP = CO × PR, and because CO = HR × SV,

MAP = HR × SV × PR

When heart rate, stroke volume or peripheral resistance rises, MAP rises.

• SV is affected by venous return (EDV)

• HR is maintained by medullary centers

• R is affected mostly by vessel diameter

Short-term BP control works by changing those three. Find the medulla: that is the HR/vasomotor office. Find the aorta and internal carotid: those walls are stretch sensors. Find the suprarenal gland: that is the epinephrine dump.

check.q: Write the MAP equation and name what mainly sets SV, HR and R.
check.a: MAP = HR × SV × PR. SV: venous return (EDV). HR: medullary centers. R: mostly vessel diameter.

steps.title: Baroreceptor reflex: the daily controller
steps.text:
Baroreceptor reflexes: a change in BP produces changes in PR, HR and SV (all three MAP ingredients).

When pressure rises, aortic and carotid walls stretch, baroreceptors fire more, and the medulla raises vagal (cardioinhibitory) output and lowers sympathetic tone. HR falls, SV falls, vessels dilate (PR falls), and BP comes down. A fall in BP runs every arrow the other way.

In most circumstances throughout the day, the baroreceptor reflex is the most important for maintaining BP. The atlas landmarks are the aorta and internal carotid artery (stretch) and the medulla oblongata (the centre). The vagus is the parasympathetic brake on HR.

check.q: What does a baroreceptor reflex change, and when is it the main BP control?
check.a: It changes PR, HR and SV. It is the most important day-to-day mechanism.

steps.title: Adrenal medullary mechanism
steps.text:
The adrenal medullary mechanism results from a substantial increase in sympathetic stimulation of heart and blood vessels. Triggers include a fall in BP, exercise, and stress.

The suprarenal (adrenal) medulla releases epinephrine and norepinephrine, which mimic sympathetic stimulation (raise HR, SV and vasoconstriction).

This mechanism plays a role during exercise and emergencies, not as the quiet daily tweak (that is baroreceptors).

check.q: What does the adrenal medulla release, and when does this mechanism matter?
check.a: Epinephrine and norepinephrine (they mimic sympathetic stimulation). Exercise and emergencies (also when BP falls).

steps.title: Chemoreceptor reflexes
steps.text:
Chemoreceptor reflexes are sensitive to oxygen, CO2 and pH levels of blood.

They are more important when blood O2 falls: high altitudes, or when CO2 rises or pH falls.

Low O2, high CO2 or acidosis is treated as an emergency for flow: the reflex raises drive to breathe and supports BP so the brain still gets perfusion. It is not the main daily BP loop in a resting person at sea level.

check.q: Chemoreceptors sense which three blood variables, and when do they matter most for BP?
