check.a: O₂, CO₂ and pH. Most important when O₂ is low (high altitude) or CO₂ is high or pH is low.

steps.title: CNS ischemic response: last ditch
steps.text:
The central nervous system ischemic response results from lack of blood flow to the medulla oblongata. Vasomotor neurons then stimulate vasoconstriction to raise BP.

It is activated only in emergency conditions when the brain receives too little O2. It is not a daily reflex. If MAP has fallen so far that the medulla itself is ischemic, this is a last attempt to squeeze the periphery and save the brain.

Summary: baroreceptors all day; adrenal medulla in exercise and emergencies; chemoreceptors when gases or pH are wrong; CNS ischemic only when the medulla is underperfused.

check.q: What triggers the CNS ischemic response, and what does it do?
check.a: Lack of blood flow to the medulla; vasomotor neurons vasoconstrict to raise BP. Emergency only.

practice.q: MAP equals…
practice.why: MAP = CO × PR = HR × SV × PR.

practice.q: From adolescence to middle age, MAP is about…
practice.why: About 70 at birth, 100 adolescence to middle age, 110 in healthy older people.

practice.q: The most important day-to-day BP mechanism is the…
practice.why: Throughout the day the baroreceptor reflex is most important.

practice.q: Baroreceptors monitor…
choices: Stretch and change in BP in vessel walls
practice.why: Myelinated sensory fibers as baroreceptors: stretch and ΔBP, especially aorta and carotid.

practice.q: Epinephrine and norepinephrine from the adrenal medulla…
choices: Are released from the kidney JGA
practice.why: They mimic sympathetic stimulation in exercise, emergencies, or a fall in BP.

practice.q: The CNS ischemic response is triggered by…
choices: Lack of blood flow to the medulla oblongata
practice.why: Medullary ischemia: last-ditch vasoconstriction to raise BP.

practice.q: Order short-term mechanisms from everyday to last-ditch emergency.
items: Chemoreceptors (low O₂ / high CO₂ / low pH)

practice.q: Why is MAP slightly less than the arithmetic mean of systolic and diastolic?
practice.a: Because diastole lasts longer than systole.

practice.q: What mainly determines SV, HR and R in the MAP equation?
practice.a: SV: venous return (EDV). HR: medullary centers. R: mostly vessel diameter.

title: Long-term blood pressure: kidney, RAAS, ANH and fluid shift
summary: Kidneys set volume, the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone cascade, atrial natriuretic hormone, fluid shift and stress-relaxation.
objectives: Explain how urine volume directly changes blood volume and MAP
Trace RAAS from low BP to angiotensin II, aldosterone and ACE inhibitors
Describe ANH as the opposite of RAAS
Outline fluid-shift and stress-relaxation responses
takeaways: Kidneys: MAP and volume up → urine up → volume and BP down. The reverse when volume is low. Some long-term mechanisms start in minutes and last hours to days.

Low BP → kidney releases renin → angiotensinogen (liver) to angiotensin I → ACE (lungs) to angiotensin II → vasoconstriction + aldosterone (kidney keeps Na+ and water) → volume and BP rise. ACE inhibitors treat hypertension.
ANH from atrial muscle when venous return stretches the atria: more urine and Na+ loss, vasodilation, PR down, BP down.
Fluid shift: extra capillary pressure pushes fluid into interstitium (a reservoir); low BP pulls it back. Stress-relaxation: smooth muscle slowly resets tone when volume changes over many minutes.

steps.title: Long-term control is mostly volume
steps.text:
Short-term reflexes change HR, SV and diameter in seconds. Long-term regulation is:

• regulation of blood concentration and volume by the kidneys

• movement of fluid across vessel walls

• alterations in the volume of blood vessels themselves

Some of these begin in minutes and keep working for hours, days or longer. The kidney is the slow, powerful volume knob.

check.q: Name three long-term BP strategies from the lecture.
check.a: Kidney control of blood concentration and volume; fluid movement across vessel walls; altering the volume of blood vessels.

steps.title: The kidney's direct effect on urine volume
steps.text:
The kidneys regulate BP by altering blood volume through urine production.

As blood volume and MAP rise, urine volume rises. More urine out means blood volume and BP fall.

If blood volume and BP fall, urine production falls. Less urine out means volume and BP can rise again.

No hormone names yet: this is the kidney acting as a faucet. Hormones (next steps) bias that faucet.

check.q: If MAP rises, what happens to urine volume and then to BP?
check.a: Urine volume increases; losing that fluid lowers blood volume and BP.

steps.title: RAAS: renin to angiotensin II
steps.text:
Renin release depends on BP: renin is released when BP falls, and release falls when BP rises.

Follow the diagram:

• The liver makes angiotensinogen. Renin converts it to angiotensin I.

• ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme, in the lungs) converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II.

• Angiotensin II causes vasoconstriction and stimulates aldosterone, so the kidney keeps Na+ and water. Volume rises, BP rises.

ACE inhibitors are a class of drugs used to treat hypertension: they block the I → II step, so this cascade cannot raise BP as hard.

check.q: When is renin released, and what do ACE inhibitors block?
check.a: When BP falls. ACE inhibitors block conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II and are used for hypertension.

steps.title: ANH: the opposite hormone from the atria
steps.text:
Atrial natriuretic hormone (ANH) is released from cardiac muscle cells in the atria when venous return increases (the atria stretch).

ANH acts on the kidneys to increase urine production and Na+ loss, and it dilates arteries and veins.

Loss of water and Na+ → blood volume down, venous return down. Vasodilation → PR down. Both drop BP.

If RAAS is the 'volume up' cascade, ANH is the 'volume down' hormone from the heart itself.

check.q: What releases ANH, and what two effects lower BP?
check.a: Stretched atrial muscle when venous return is high. More urine/Na⁺ loss (volume down) and vasodilation (PR down).

steps.title: Fluid-shift mechanism
steps.text:
The fluid-shift mechanism responds to small changes in capillary blood pressure.

As BP rises, some fluid is forced from capillaries into interstitial spaces. As BP falls, interstitial fluid moves back into capillaries and resists a further fall.

Interstitial volume acts as a reservoir in equilibrium with a large volume of intracellular fluid. The mechanism begins immediately but needs hours to reach full effect. That is why dehydration is not an acute problem in the first minutes: the reservoir buffers it.

check.q: How does fluid shift protect BP, and how fast is it?
check.a: High BP: fluid leaves capillaries into interstitium. Low BP: fluid returns. It starts at once but takes hours to finish; it buffers dehydration.

steps.title: Stress-relaxation, and ADH as a textbook neighbour
steps.text:
The stress-relaxation response is a vasomotor adjustment of blood vessels to a change in blood volume. When volume (and pressure) suddenly fall, smooth muscle contracts; when volume rises, it slowly relaxes. It is most effective when the BP change occurs over many minutes.

The posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis) is on the diagram as a related long-term hormone source: ADH (vasopressin) is released when BP falls a lot or osmolality rises, so the kidney keeps water and vessels constrict. The lecture's own named long-term list is kidney volume, RAAS, ANH, fluid shift and stress-relaxation; ADH sits beside them in the figure.

check.q: What is stress-relaxation of vessels?
check.a: Smooth muscle slowly contracts when volume/pressure fall and relaxes when they rise; it works best over many minutes.

practice.q: If blood volume and MAP fall, urine production…
choices: Decreases, helping volume and BP rise
practice.why: Low volume/BP → less urine → volume and BP can recover.

practice.q: Renin is released when…
practice.why: Renin when BP falls; less renin when BP rises.

practice.q: ACE inhibitors treat hypertension by blocking…
choices: Conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II
practice.why: ACE converts I to II; blocking it is a hypertension treatment.

practice.q: ANH is released from…
choices: Atrial cardiac muscle when venous return stretches the atria
The adrenal medulla only in shock
practice.why: Atrial stretch (↑ venous return) → ANH → more urine/Na⁺ and vasodilation → BP down.

practice.q: The fluid-shift mechanism is why…
choices: Dehydration is not an acute problem
Pulse pressure is measured at the radial artery
practice.why: Interstitial fluid is a reservoir; the shift starts at once but takes hours, buffering dehydration.

practice.q: Order the RAAS cascade when BP falls.
items: Vasoconstriction and aldosterone (Na⁺ and water kept)

practice.q: Name two ANH effects that lower BP.
practice.a: Increased urine and Na⁺ loss (volume down) and vasodilation (PR down).

practice.q: What protein does renin act on, and where is that protein made?
practice.a: Angiotensinogen, made by the liver.

title: Tissue blood flow and five kinds of shock
summary: Muscle 1 versus 10 L/min, brain 750 mL/min and MAP limits, plus hypovolemic, neurogenic, anaphylactic, septic and cardiogenic shock.
objectives: Give resting and exercise skeletal-muscle flow
Give brain flow and the MAP limits for syncope and cerebral edema
Define circulatory shock and list five types with causes
takeaways: Skeletal muscle: about 1 L/min at rest (myogenic and neural); up to about 10 L/min in exercise (metabolic).
Brain: must stay about 750 mL/min. Low pH or high CO2 dilates cerebral vessels. Low MAP dilates, high MAP constricts (myogenic). MAP < 60 → syncope; MAP > 160 → cerebral edema.
Shock = inadequate flow that damages tissues (failure to keep normal BP).

Five: hypovolemic (volume: bleed, burns, diarrhea, vomiting, dehydration); neurogenic/vascular (vasodilation: stress, anesthesia); anaphylactic (histamine, leaky capillaries); septic (infection/toxins: vasodilation and leaky capillaries); cardiogenic (CO down: MI, fibrillation, arrhythmia, electrical shock).

steps.title: Flow matches the tissue's need, plus new vessels
steps.text:
In most tissues, flow is proportional to metabolic needs (local control). The nervous system routes blood and holds BP. Hormones (epinephrine, norepinephrine) add a whole-body layer.

If a tissue needs more flow for a long time it can grow new vessels: angiogenesis.

Two organs get special numbers: skeletal muscle (wildly variable) and brain (stubbornly constant).

check.q: What is angiogenesis in this lecture?
check.a: Production of new vessels to meet tissue needs.

steps.title: Skeletal muscle: 1 L/min versus 10 L/min
steps.text:
Skeletal-muscle flow varies with fiber type and activity.

At rest: myogenic and neural mechanisms predominate. Flow is maintained at about 1 L/min.

In activity/exercise: flow increases in proportion to metabolic activity and can increase 10-fold, to about 10 L/min.

That is why muscle capillary networks are dense, and why arterioles and sphincters have to open on demand. The extra 9 L/min has to come from a higher CO (remember 5 to 25 L/min in the aorta in exercise) and from redirecting flow.

check.q: What is skeletal-muscle blood flow at rest and in heavy exercise?
check.a: About 1 L/min at rest; about 10 L/min (a 10-fold rise) in exercise.

steps.title: Brain: 750 mL/min, or syncope and edema
steps.text:
Brain flow must be constant, about 750 mL/min, because neurons are intolerant of ischemia.

Metabolic controls: vasodilation in response to low pH or high CO2.

Myogenic controls: if MAP falls, cerebral vessels dilate; if MAP rises, they constrict (protecting the capillary bed).

MAP below 60 mm Hg can lead to syncope (fainting). MAP above 160 mm Hg can lead to cerebral edema.

check.q: Give the brain's required flow and the MAP values linked to syncope and cerebral edema.
check.a: About 750 mL/min. MAP < 60 mm Hg: syncope. MAP > 160 mm Hg: cerebral edema.

steps.title: Circulatory shock: five names
steps.text:
Circulatory shock is inadequate blood flow that causes tissue damage (failure to maintain normal BP). Any of the five types can kill if MAP is not restored.

Memorise the five with one cause-phrase each:

1. Hypovolemic - volume too low

2. Neurogenic (vascular) - vessels too wide

3. Anaphylactic - allergy, leaky capillaries

4. Septic - infection and toxins

5. Cardiogenic - the pump fails

check.q: Define circulatory shock and name the five types.
check.a: Inadequate flow that damages tissues. Hypovolemic, neurogenic (vascular), anaphylactic, septic, cardiogenic.

steps.title: Hypovolemic, neurogenic and anaphylactic
steps.text:
Hypovolemic shock is reduced blood volume: severe bleeding; burns; diarrhea, vomiting, dehydration.

Neurogenic (vascular) shock is vasodilation: emotional stress; anesthesia. The tank is not empty; the pipes are too large, so pressure collapses.

Anaphylactic shock is an allergic response. A histamine dump causes increased capillary permeability (plasma leaves the vessels).

check.q: Give one cause each for hypovolemic, neurogenic and anaphylactic shock.
check.a: Hypovolemic: bleeding, burns, diarrhea, vomiting or dehydration. Neurogenic: emotional stress or anesthesia (vasodilation). Anaphylactic: allergy with histamine and leaky capillaries.

steps.title: Septic and cardiogenic
steps.text:
Septic shock is caused by infection and toxins. Vasodilation, increased permeability and disordered tissue perfusion are central. The lecture lists decreased HR, but tachycardia is common; a low HR is not a defining requirement.

Cardiogenic shock is a decrease in cardiac output: MI; fibrillations and arrhythmias; electrical shocks. The volume may be normal and the vessels may be able to constrict, but the pump cannot generate MAP.

Critical closing pressure from earlier matters here: if MAP falls below the closing pressure of arterioles, flow to tissues can stop even before the heart fully does.
steps.clinical: Cardiogenic shock after MI is a pump problem. Fluids that help hypovolemia can overload a failed left ventricle.

check.q: What causes septic shock versus cardiogenic shock?
check.a: Septic: infection-associated dysregulated response with vasodilation and permeability changes. Cardiogenic: inadequate pump output, for example after myocardial injury.

practice.q: Resting skeletal-muscle blood flow is about…
practice.why: About 1 L/min at rest; ~10 L/min in exercise.

practice.q: Brain blood flow must stay about…
practice.why: Neurons need a constant ~750 mL/min.

practice.q: MAP below 60 mm Hg can cause…
practice.why: MAP < 60 → syncope; MAP > 160 → cerebral edema.

practice.q: Hypovolemic shock is from…
practice.why: Volume loss: bleeding, burns, diarrhea, vomiting, dehydration.

practice.q: Neurogenic (vascular) shock results from…
practice.why: Pipes too wide: emotional stress or anesthesia.

practice.q: Anaphylactic shock involves…
choices: A histamine dump and increased capillary permeability
Only a fall in hematocrit from bleeding
practice.why: Allergy → histamine → leaky capillaries.

practice.q: Cardiogenic shock is…
choices: A drop in CO (MI, fibrillation, arrhythmia, electrical shock)
practice.why: The pump fails, so CO (and MAP) fall.

practice.q: Match each shock to its one-line cause, in this order: hypovolemic, neurogenic, anaphylactic, septic, cardiogenic.
What MAP values are linked to syncope and to cerebral edema?
practice.a: MAP < 60 mm Hg: syncope. MAP > 160 mm Hg: cerebral edema.

practice.q: What happens to cerebral vessels if MAP falls? If MAP rises?
practice.a: Fall in MAP: dilation. Rise in MAP: constriction (myogenic). Low pH or high CO₂ also dilates (metabolic).

title: Fetal shunts, aging arteries, hypotension and hypertension
summary: Fetal shunts and the fossa ovalis, arteriosclerosis versus atherosclerosis, and the lecture's hypo- and hypertension labels.
objectives: Name the three fetal shunts and the adult remnant of the foramen ovale
Contrast arteriosclerosis with atherosclerosis
Define hypotension and hypertension as in this lecture, including subtypes
takeaways: Mesoderm → endothelial lining. Fetal shunts: foramen ovale, ductus arteriosus, ductus venosus; plus umbilical vein and arteries. Foramen ovale becomes the fossa ovalis.
Arteriosclerosis: arteries less elastic (degenerative). Atherosclerosis: plaque on walls of medium and larger arteries, including coronaries.

Hypotension: systolic < 100 mm Hg (orthostatic, chronic, acute/shock). Hypertension in this section: systolic > 160 mm Hg (transient vs chronic; primary vs secondary). Table 21.14 used lower modern cutoffs; know both.
Aging also brings varicose veins. Extrinsic BP factors: age, sex, weight, activity, ethnicity, mood, posture, socioeconomic status.

steps.title: Development: mesoderm and fetal shunts
steps.text:
Endothelial lining comes from mesoderm. New vessels form as needed (wound healing, uterus).

The fetus does not use its lungs for gas exchange, so three shunts bypass unused beds:

• foramen ovale (right atrium to left atrium)

• ductus arteriosus (pulmonary trunk to aorta)

• ductus venosus (umbilical vein blood past the liver toward the IVC)

Plus umbilical veins and arteries to the placenta. The diagram traces the whole fetal route; this lecture needs the three names and what they skip.

check.q: Name the three fetal shunts.
check.a: Foramen ovale, ductus arteriosus and ductus venosus.

steps.title: Foramen ovale becomes the fossa ovalis
steps.text:
In the fetus, much of the blood entering the right atrium crosses the foramen ovale into the left atrium, skipping the lungs.

After birth, left atrial pressure rises, the flap closes, and the remnant is the fossa ovalis in the interatrial septum. Find it on the whole-heart model.

The other remnants (for lab, not required as atlas names here): ductus arteriosus → ligamentum arteriosum; ductus venosus → ligamentum venosum; umbilical vein → round ligament of the liver.

The model highlights the interatrial septum; the fossa ovalis is not a separately labeled part in this model.

check.q: What adult structure is the remnant of the foramen ovale?
check.a: The fossa ovalis.

steps.title: Arteriosclerosis versus atherosclerosis
steps.text:
Do not treat these as the same word.

Arteriosclerosis: degenerative changes in arteries making them less elastic ('hardening'). Compliance falls, pulse pressure rises (you already used that).

Atherosclerosis: deposition of plaque on walls. It affects medium and larger arteries, including coronary arteries.

Aging of vessels in the lecture also lists hypertension, atherosclerosis and varicose veins as common late problems. The plaque diagram shows intimal plaque deep to the endothelium, narrowing the lumen.
steps.pitfall: Arteriosclerosis = loss of elasticity. Atherosclerosis = plaque. Atherosclerosis is a common way to get arteriosclerotic (stiff, narrow) arteries, but the definitions are not identical.

check.q: Contrast arteriosclerosis with atherosclerosis.
check.a: Arteriosclerosis: arteries become less elastic. Atherosclerosis: plaque on the walls of medium and larger arteries (including coronaries).

steps.title: Hypotension
steps.text:
In this section, hypotension is low BP with systolic below 100 mm Hg.

Three flavours:

• Orthostatic: temporary (the head rush after standing)

• Chronic: poor nutrition; Addison's disease; hypothyroid

• Acute: a sign of circulatory shock

Orthostatic hypotension is gravity plus sluggish short-term reflexes: blood is below the heart, MAP at the brain dips, you sway. The baroreflex usually catches it.

check.q: What systolic value defines hypotension here, and what is orthostatic hypotension?
check.a: Systolic < 100 mm Hg. Orthostatic: a temporary drop on standing (head rush).

steps.title: Hypertension
steps.text:
In this same section, hypertension is high BP with systolic above 160 mm Hg. That is an older cutoff than Table 21.14 (where Stage 2 already starts at 140 or 90, and crisis at 180/120). Learn the table for classes and this paragraph for the lecture's clinical labels.

Transient: fever; physical exertion; emotional stress.

Chronic: damage to vessels, baroreceptors, heart muscle or vascular organs.

Chronic splits into primary (heredity, stress, smoking) and secondary (the result of other disorders).

check.q: What systolic value is hypertension in this lecture section, and what is primary versus secondary chronic hypertension?
check.a: Systolic > 160 mm Hg. Primary: heredity, stress, smoking. Secondary: caused by other disorders.

steps.title: Extrinsic factors that affect BP
steps.text:
The lecture's non-disease list of things that affect BP:

age, sex, weight, physical activity, ethnicity (hereditary factors), mood, posture, socioeconomic status (access to nutrition).

You already have the machinery: compliance falling with age, posture and gravity, exercise raising CO, mood and stress using the adrenal medulla, nutrition affecting chronic hypotension. This list is the reminder that MAP is not only a vessel-wall number.

check.q: Name four extrinsic factors that affect BP from the lecture list.
check.a: Any four of: age, sex, weight, physical activity, ethnicity, mood, posture, socioeconomic status (nutrition access).

practice.q: The three fetal shunts are…
choices: Foramen ovale, ductus arteriosus and ductus venosus
practice.why: Foramen ovale, ductus arteriosus, ductus venosus (plus umbilical vessels to the placenta).

practice.q: The fossa ovalis is the remnant of the…
practice.why: The closed foramen ovale leaves the fossa ovalis.

practice.q: Arteriosclerosis is…
practice.why: Arteriosclerosis: arteries become less elastic. Atherosclerosis is plaque.

practice.q: Atherosclerosis is…
choices: Only loss of elasticity with no plaque
Deposition of plaque on walls of medium and larger arteries
practice.why: Plaque on medium and larger arteries, including coronaries.

practice.q: In this lecture section, hypotension is systolic…
practice.why: Hypotension: systolic < 100 mm Hg.

practice.q: In this lecture section, hypertension is systolic…
practice.why: This section's hypertension label is systolic > 160 (Table 21.14 uses different modern cutoffs).

practice.q: Acute hypotension is a sign of…
practice.why: Acute hypotension flags shock.

practice.q: Order fetal structures as they bypass unused beds, matching: RA to LA, pulmonary trunk to aorta, umbilical vein past liver.
What adult remnant marks the fetal foramen ovale?
practice.a: The fossa ovalis on the interatrial septum.

practice.q: Name three causes of chronic hypotension from the lecture.
practice.a: Poor nutrition, Addison's disease, hypothyroidism.

practice.q: Primary chronic hypertension is associated with which three factors?
practice.a: Heredity, stress and smoking.
